lab_title: The Retrograde Puzzle: Earth, Mars, and the Heliocentric Revolution
top_level_objectives: Describe the apparent retrograde motion of Mars as observed from Earth's surface over several months.
Explain the mechanics of Ptolemy's geocentric epicycles and why they were historically used to explain retrograde motion.
Demonstrate how the heliocentric model explains retrograde motion as an optical illusion caused by Earth overtaking outer planets.
Relate the physical distance of outer planets (Mars, Jupiter, Saturn) to the visual scale of their retrograde loops.

scenes.brief_purpose: Introduce students to the phenomenon of apparent retrograde motion as observed from the surface of Earth against the background of stars.
key_visuals: A semi-dome projection of the night sky showing familiar constellations (such as Taurus and Gemini) on the horizon.
A bright red sphere representing Mars.
A timeline overlay indicating dates over a 6-month period.
A glowing trail that slowly traces Mars's path across the celestial sphere, showing a distinct loop-the-loop shape.
student_actions: Drag a time slider to advance the calendar night-by-night.
Observe Mars drifting slowly eastward, slowing to a stop, reversing direction (retrograde) for several weeks, and then resuming its normal eastward path.
Place interactive flags on the dates when Mars enters and exits the retrograde loop.

scenes.brief_purpose: Explore the historical geocentric explanation of retrograde motion using Ptolemy's system of epicycles.
key_visuals: A 3D tabletop model of the geocentric universe with Earth stationary at the absolute center.
Mars riding on a small, spinning orbital circle (the epicycle).
The center of the epicycle riding on a larger orbital circle (the deferent) around Earth.
A trace line showing how this compound circular motion draws a loop from Earth's central viewpoint.
student_actions: Rotate the 3D model in AR to view it from above.
Adjust a dial to change the rotation speed of Mars's epicycle relative to its deferent.
Observe how complex the system must be to match real-world observations, noting how the geocentric model struggles with simplicity.

scenes.brief_purpose: Transition to the heliocentric model to view the simple, uninterrupted circular orbits of Earth and Mars around the Sun.
key_visuals: A tabletop 3D model of the inner solar system with a glowing Sun at the center.
Earth and Mars on concentric, coplanar orbits, moving continuously in the same counter-clockwise direction with no epicycles.
Earth moving visibly faster in its inner orbit than Mars in its outer orbit.
student_actions: Walk around the solar system model to inspect it from different angles, observing the lack of loops in the physical orbits.
Compare the relative speeds of Earth and Mars by timing how long each takes to complete a single orbit.
Acknowledge that retrograde loops do not physically occur in space, setting up the question of how the illusion is created.

scenes.brief_purpose: Demonstrate how the relative motion of Earth overtaking Mars naturally creates the illusion of retrograde motion using a line-of-sight projection.
key_visuals: The heliocentric 3D model of Earth and Mars orbiting the Sun.
A dynamic, glowing "line of sight" projecting from Earth, passing straight through Mars, and landing on a distant curved screen representing the background stars.
Numbered markers (1 through 5) along Earth's and Mars's orbits, indicating matching dates as Earth catches up to and passes Mars.
student_actions: Step through the numbered markers one by one, watching the Earth physically catch up to and pass Mars.
Observe how the projection of the sight line on the distant screen sweeps backward (westward) during the passing phase (markers 2 to 4), tracing the exact loop observed in Scene 1.

Interact with a "passing car" analogy mini-game where the student drives a fast car passing a slower car on a highway, observing how the slower car appears to drift backward against distant mountains.

scenes.brief_purpose: Extend the heliocentric explanation to other outer planets to understand how distance impacts the scale and duration of retrograde loops.
key_visuals: An expanded 3D heliocentric model including the orbits of Earth, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.
Projected line-of-sight paths for all three outer planets projected onto the distant stellar background.
A comparison chart showing orbit sizes, orbital periods, and the relative size of each planet's retrograde loop.
student_actions: Toggle sight lines for Jupiter and Saturn on and off.
Run the simulation and observe that Jupiter and Saturn also undergo retrograde motion, but their loops are narrower and less pronounced because they are much farther away from Earth.
Match planets to their respective retrograde loops on a quiz board based on their distance from the Sun.
